text: You look away for ten seconds, and the milk is all over the stove. But a pot of water never does that. Why?
Milk is almost ninety percent water. The rest is fat, sugar and proteins. And those proteins are the troublemakers.
As the milk heats up, some proteins unfold and join with the fat at the top. Together they make a thin skin.
When it boils, steam bubbles rise. In water, they simply pop at the surface. In milk, the skin and the proteins hold them in.
So the bubbles pile up into a foam. More heat means more steam, and the foam climbs fast, right over the edge.
Turn off the flame, and the steam stops. The bubbles shrink, and the foam sinks back down in seconds.
So keep the flame low, stir now and then to break the skin, and use a bigger pot.
